A policy sentence that specifies non-sale for a subset of consumers while implying sales for others contributes to the overall description of the right to opt out, because it clarifies the conditions under which the right can or cannot be invoked.

When a disclosure explains that a particular category of consumers is not subject to data selling, that explanation is part of characterizing the opt-out right, as it defines the population for whom the right is relevant or automatically satisfied.

A sentence that explicitly commits an entity to refrain from differential treatment or retaliation against individuals for asserting their legal rights directly articulates the non-discrimination guarantee.
A statement that references a specific data protection statute while guaranteeing no adverse action for exercising rights ties the text to that statute's anti-discrimination provision.
Sentences that promise uniformity in pricing, service, or quality regardless of whether a user exercises data rights are clear markers of the non-discrimination right.

When a sentence uses a direct first-person corporate voice ("we") to address the consumer about protections, it functions as a policy statement that conveys a right rather than a mere factual description.

A sentence that specifies a purpose for data handling, such as conducting internal analytics, signals that behavioral or usage data is being collected, thereby defining a category of personal information.
Descriptions of processing activities without explicit data fields imply the categories by inference, where the stated function (analytics) directly corresponds to a type of personal data acquired.
Mentioning the website operator as the actor clarifies that the collection occurs for first-party operational aims, which still constitutes a personal-information category in disclosure contexts.
Phrasing that links data usage to measurement or analysis indicates the gathering of user interaction metrics, which falls under the scope of collected personal information categories.

A sentence that explicitly enumerates actionable steps a consumer can take to enforce a legally defined privacy right, such as using a specific web form, emailing a designated address, or calling a toll-free number, is labeled as a method to exercise that right.

A sentence that pairs a legal compliance reference (e.g., CCPA) with an action taken for consumer requests is characterizing how the covered right is operationalized, making it a statement about that right.

Statements that give the reader direct, operational instructions about how to trigger a privacy protection are categorized as methods, in contrast to sentences that merely state that a right exists or define its scope.

The inclusion of multiple alternative contact mechanisms (web link, email subject line, phone number) indicates the sentence is providing the means for the consumer to act, which is characteristic of a method for exercising rights.

When a sentence frames the user as able to 'opt out' or 'submit a request' and pairs that framing with concrete procedural channels, it functions as an instruction manual for invoking the right rather than merely describing the right itself.
A sentence that connects a verification challenge to the risk of disclosing sensitive records to an unauthorized person illustrates a justification for limiting the right to know.
A sentence that depicts a plausible scenario where multiple individuals may have access to a device without clear ownership helps define the conditions under which the right to know can be exercised.

A sentence that explains why an organization cannot verify that the requester is the actual owner of the personal information at issue clarifies the boundaries of the right to access one's personal information.

A sentence that introduces a concrete example using a transitional phrase like 'for instance' to illustrate a practical limitation on disclosing personal information is part of describing the right to know what personal information is collected.

A sentence that appears within a block of text dedicated to explaining how to exercise privacy rights is labeled accordingly, regardless of whether its content is a heading or an address, because the surrounding context defines its role.

A sentence that specifies concrete contact channels such as an email address and a postal mailing address for submitting privacy-related requests is providing actionable methods to exercise those rights.

A heading that names categories of entities involved in data processing, such as service providers or trusted partners, is considered part of the methods to exercise rights when it appears in a section that also lists contact channels for exercising those rights.

In a document that enumerates multiple ways to contact an organization (email, phone, mail), any sentence containing contact details—even if it is just an address—is treated as a method to exercise rights because it contributes to the set of available submission channels.

A sentence that references the handling, removal, or consent for personal information of a specific resident group is categorized under the types of information collected because it implicitly enumerates the categories of data subject to those actions.
Mentioning a specific privacy regulation (such as the CCPA) that mandates disclosures about sales or sharing signals that the sentence falls under the topic of sold personal information categories.

The presence of terms like 'personal information' and a named jurisdiction (e.g., California residents) signals that the sentence belongs to a discussion of the categories of data the policy collects and manages.

A sentence describing steps taken after learning that certain personal information was collected is part of the lifecycle of that information, which is a core aspect of defining the categories of information collected.

When a sentence mentions legally required consent for processing personal information, it is grouped under the categories of information collected because consent is tied to the specific types of data being processed.

A sentence that reserves the right to modify a policy at any time, specifies that changes take effect upon posting on a website, and does not require prior notice is a hallmark of a policy update notification.

The label 'Updated Privacy Policy' is appropriate for a sentence that serves as a temporal marker distinguishing the current version from prior ones; such markers are typically bare dates with no additional contextual prose.

A clause that explicitly states the organization's unilateral authority to amend a policy and designates a public posting as the trigger for effectiveness is characteristic of a document segment announcing policy updates.
When a text includes a reservation of rights to modify terms and frames continued use as consent, it aligns with a privacy policy update clause that alerts users to possible future changes.

A sentence that explicitly names subcategories of personal data, such as employment history and performance evaluation records, is cataloguing the types of data a collector gathers, so it belongs under a label that groups categories of personal information collected.

In a document where parallel bullet points each introduce a different data type, a sentence with the same structure that introduces another personal data type is consistently mapped to the label denoting categories of personal information collected.

An item that refers to records tied to a person's professional life, like job history and evaluations, is a recognized kind of personal information and thus fits the category of collected personal information in a privacy listing.

When a privacy disclosure enumerates distinct data kinds with the conjunction 'or' between them, the sentence is describing a single overarching data category rather than a transactional fact, warranting a label that names that category of collected information.
In a section framed by an introductory clause about permitted denials, each subsequent enumerated condition serves to complete the description of that same right.
When a disclosure enumerates statutory exceptions or permissible processing purposes, it clarifies the scope of a consumer's right to restrict, thereby describing that right.
A numbered enumeration of lawful bases for declining a request directly elaborates the conditions under which the associated consumer right does not apply.
Text explaining when a request may be denied is as central to describing a right as text explaining when it may be granted, because it specifies the right's boundaries.
A sentence that cross-references or points to a separate resource detailing the types of personal information handled by the organization is treated as a disclosure of those categories.
A sentence whose content refers to explaining the categories of personal information—even indirectly through a hyperlink or reference—is labeled for the collection categories topic.
If a sentence provides a link or a pointer to further information about the use or collection of personal data, it is categorized under the section describing what personal information is collected.
A sentence that enumerates lawful uses for retaining personal information explains an exception or limitation to a deletion request, thereby describing the boundaries of the right to delete.

A clause allowing internal uses that are compatible with the original context specifies a condition under which a business may lawfully keep data after a deletion demand, which is a core element of how the right to delete is scoped.

When a sentence appears in a numbered list alongside other legal carve-outs (e.g., security, compliance, contractual obligations), it functions as part of a comprehensive description of when the right to delete is not absolute.
A declarative sentence that ties the absence of discrimination to the act of invoking legal rights under a privacy statute indicates a description of the non-discrimination right.
When a sentence directly affirms that exercising one's privacy rights will not lead to discriminatory treatment, it functions as a statement of the non-discrimination guarantee.

The presence of a label referencing non-discrimination together with a clear commitment not to retaliate against rights exercise signals that the sentence articulates this specific consumer protection.

A sentence that functions as a section heading introducing a list of prohibited retaliatory or differential treatments of consumers who exercise their privacy rights is appropriately labeled as a description of the right to non-discrimination.
A sentence that outlines the terms for voluntary participation in an incentive program reinforces that no penalty or denial is imposed for declining, which is core to a non-discrimination guarantee.
Stating that an action requires prior consent, and that the consent is revocable at any time, clarifies the boundary of a permissible exception to an otherwise prohibited differential treatment.
The statement's focus on user choice and control over participation aligns with the principle that protected rights cannot be conditioned on forfeiting one's own protections.
When a statement defines a right by prohibiting adverse treatment in response to exercising other rights, it describes the right to non-discrimination.

A sentence that describes the specific data practices involving third-party advertising services is often included to provide context for a consumer's right to opt out of the sale or sharing of personal information.

A description of a right to opt out of the sale of personal information often clarifies that exercising the right does not eliminate all related advertising, including interest-based ads, thereby setting expectations about the scope of the opt-out.

Sentences that describe an opt-out pathway for interest-based advertising are categorized as methods to exercise rights, as they inform users how to assert their privacy preference over the handling of their data.
The presence of an actionable instruction to exercise an opt-out choice indicates that the sentence provides a procedural description of an opt-out right, which falls under the given label.

A sentence that enumerates specific prohibited acts of differential treatment (denying services, varying prices, or altering quality) characteristically serves as a description of a non-discrimination right.
Listing concrete examples of discriminatory actions makes the abstract right to non-discrimination tangible and actionable for the reader.
Referencing a governing statute's exception (here, the CCPA) frames the enumerated prohibitions as conditional and legally bounded rather than absolute.
Using a direct prohibitory structure ('we will not') in a list format clearly communicates the obligation imposed on the data collector regarding consumer rights.

A sentence that conditions the exercise of the deletion right on whether the information is still needed for the ongoing relationship or processing user requests helps delineate the scope of the right.
Descriptions of deletion rights usually include an explicit exception clause that allows the business to retain data under certain defined circumstances, reflecting that the right is not absolute.
A statement that connects retention obligations to service providers and legal requirements elaborates on the practical application of a data privacy deletion right.
Statements that clarify the boundaries of the deletion right by referencing business-purpose justifications are characteristic of such descriptions.

When a privacy notice pairs a list of information categories with a statutory cross-reference to a disclosure paragraph, the sentence functions as an operational description of the right to know what personal information is held.

A sentence that enumerates the business or commercial purposes for which personal data is collected is typically classified as part of a disclosure addressing the consumer's right to know about the collection, use, sale, or sharing of their information.

A passage that clarifies specialized handling of a particular data subset (such as financial data being limited to verification and billing) reinforces that the surrounding disclosure is part of the categories-of-information framework, where exceptions and restrictions on each category's use are standard content.

The presence of terms such as 'collect' and a systematic enumeration of downstream activities (e.g., maintaining, securing, personalizing, and legal compliance) aligns with the section of a privacy policy that documents both what categories are amassed and the corresponding grounds for using those categories, making the category-collection label appropriate.

A sentence that restricts third parties from using personal information beyond a specified purpose indicates the entity retains control over how shared data is used, which relates to disclosures about data sharing practices.
Language about preventing unsolicited emails from third parties indicates active dissemination of personal data to those parties, thereby revealing the types of data subject to sale or sharing.
Mentioning that data is shared with companies and that those companies cannot use it beyond specified purposes directly references the categories of personal data involved in such transfers.

Restrictions that specify data can only be used for purposes stated in a policy signal that the personal data is being provided to external entities for business purposes, falling under categories of information sold or shared.

A sentence that frames the correction as an opportunity or ability granted to the user, rather than as an obligation of the data controller, is labeled as a description of the right to correct information.
Phrases like 'you may request' indicate a user-initiated entitlement, which is a typical marker for statements that describe a data subject's specific rights.
The use of action verbs such as 'correct' or 'update' in direct relation to personal data signals a focus on the user's correction rights.

A sentence that conditions the deletion on confirmation of a verifiable request and acknowledges exceptions addresses the procedural requirements and limitations that define how the deletion right is applied, marking it as a description of the right itself.

A sentence that details the procedural steps for exercising a deletion right, including the verification of the request and the consequent deletion of personal information, directly describes that right.
A sentence that explains that deletion will occur unless a legal exemption applies frames the deletion right within its permissible boundaries, which is typical of such descriptions.
A sentence that outlines the operational workflow for honoring a deletion request, from confirmation to removal from records, serves as a description of the right to delete.

A sentence that specifies the responsible parties for deletion—both the data controller and its service providers—and conditions the action on a confirmed user request is a hallmark of a deletion-right description.
A sentence that frames the policy as something that may be updated over time directly reflects the topic of an updated privacy policy, as it acknowledges the possibility of future changes.

Statements that instruct users to check the policy on each visit in case they overlooked announcements of revisions signal that the policy is subject to continuous updates and that the latest version is the relevant one.
Explicit guidance for users to verify whether a policy has been altered is typically part of the communication mechanism for policy revisions, reinforcing the update-focused label.
Language encouraging users to monitor a document for modifications is a common feature of an update notice section, which explains how users will be informed of future revisions.
A claim that mentions storing user preferences or content details is generally classified as informing about the categories of personal information collected because it names concrete data types.
A sentence that identifies specific technologies or mechanisms used to store or capture user data typically falls under a description of the categories of information collected.
Statements naming the types of data elements involved—such as content preferences—signal that the text is enumerating the kinds of personal information gathered.
When a statement explains how user-related information is persisted or gathered, it functions as a disclosure of the categories of data the organization collects.
A sentence that explicitly grants users the ability to request verification, correction, or updating of their personal data directly describes a data-subject right focused on data accuracy.
When the action specified is a modification of stored personal data, such as correcting it, the sentence directly corresponds to the legal right to rectification.
The presence of action verbs such as 'verify,' 'correct,' or 'update' tied to 'Personal Data' signals that the statement is articulating a corrective or rectification right.
When a sentence frames the action as something the user 'may request,' it is stating an entitlement or right rather than a mere policy procedure.
A sentence that enumerates the types of data collected (e.g., activity, preferences, inferred attributes) is categorized as disclosing the categories of personal information involved.
Descriptions of data collection for feature functionality indicate the sentence is classifying the kinds of personal information handled.
Mentioning technical identifiers and tracking mechanisms signals that the text is specifying what personal information is collected or shared.
When a sentence lists concrete examples of user-related data, it serves to define the scope of personal information categories.
A sentence that describes an action to modify existing information because it is stale or inaccurate directly expresses the data subject's right to rectify personal data.
A sentence that explicitly names an action to fix or revise data that is stale or erroneous is characteristically classified as a description of a right to correct information.
A statement that focuses on the maintenance of data quality through removal of falsehoods or outdatedness is a canonical expression of an informational correction entitlement.
Statements that frame an ability or obligation to amend data when it fails to reflect current truth are categorized as descriptions of the right to correction.

The co-occurrence of verbs denoting modification (e.g., update) with adjectives indicating inaccuracy (e.g., out of date or incorrect) signals a core function of a correction right, which is to ensure data reflects current truth.
The presence of corrective verbs such as 'update' or 'correct' combined with quality flaws like outdatedness or error signals that the sentence pertains to the right to correct information.

When a sentence identifies both the defect in the information and the remedy (amending it), it aligns with the substantive scope of a right that grants individuals control over the accuracy of their data.
When a sentence specifies conditions under which stored data should be changed—namely, when it is no longer valid or contains mistakes—it is describing the right to have that data set right.

A clause that connects a specific law's authorization with a consumer's ability to inquire about their own personal information serves to inform the reader of an existing access right, fitting the label for a description of the right to know collected personal information.

When a sentence frames a privacy right as being available to individuals who meet a jurisdiction-based condition (such as being a state resident), it is typically presenting a legally conferred disclosure right rather than a general data-handling practice, aligning with a right-to-know description.

A sentence that lists categories of personal information disclosed for value and identifies the types of third parties receiving it directly describes the scope of a right-to-know request regarding sales or sharing.

A sentence that pairs 'personal information' with both collection-side details (sources, purposes) and sharing-side details (categories of third parties) maps naturally onto a right that covers information sold or shared with third parties.

The inclusion of specific disclosure elements—such as categories of information, sources, business purposes, and recipient categories—indicates that the sentence belongs to a section describing the right to know about personal information sold or shared.

When a privacy statement uses introductory phrasing like 'inform you about' to present data collection and third-party sharing details, it is usually conveying a consumer right related to the disclosure of personal information sales or transfers.

A sentence that enumerates specific purposes for which data is used implicitly identifies the categories of personal information that must be collected to fulfill those purposes.

If a text itemizes purposes like account creation, transaction processing, and security maintenance, it is effectively cataloging the categories of personal information involved, even when the wording focuses on usage rather than explicit data types.

A passage that delineates the range of activities for which personal data is used serves to inform consumers about the kinds of information that may be collected, thereby fitting the 'Categories of Personal Information Collected' classification.

When a privacy policy lists operational uses such as processing orders, preventing fraud, and personalizing content, it implicitly defines the breadth of personal information categories the organization handles, making the label applicable.
A text that enumerates the specific categories of recipients and the storage duration of personal data serves to inform data subjects about the scope and lifecycle of data disclosures.
Statements that lay out the content of information to be provided about recipients and retention periods are characteristic of privacy notices required under a right-to-know framework.
When a provision details whom data is shared with and how long it is kept, it functions as an operational specification of a data subject's right to know about transfers of their information.

A clause that includes both the parties receiving the data and the time frame of storage directly addresses the transparency obligations tied to the authorized sharing or sale of personal information.
Sentences that describe the procedural mechanism for executing an erasure request, rather than merely stating the right abstractly, are classified as descriptions of the right to delete.
The presence of an assigned role or responsible party tasked with ensuring compliance indicates the text is operationalizing a data deletion right.
The use of time-sensitive language emphasizing prompt or immediate action highlights the obligation to honor a deletion request without undue delay.
A sentence that describes a consumer's entitlement to obtain records about the transfer of personal information is a statement of a right-to-know obligation.
Distinguishing between sales and disclosures made for a business purpose indicates the text is specifying the scope of a privacy right.
A clause framed as a conditional obligation ('if we sold or disclosed') characterizes the described entitlement as a right triggered by certain data-sharing activities.
Mentioning categories of recipients in conjunction with categories of personal information signals the text explains what details a right-to-know request must include.
Specifying that the information must be provided in separate lists shows the description addresses the format and completeness of the required disclosure.

A sentence that explains a concrete operational step taken to implement a data subject's request is a description of that right, because it shows how the company gives practical effect to the limitation.
A sentence that references flagging or tagging a record in an internal system to prevent further sharing demonstrates how a restriction on processing is implemented.
Describing how a restriction is recorded or flagged in internal systems communicates the outcome of a request to limit use, thereby characterizing the right itself.
A sentence describing an internal marking practice that prevents data from being shared conveys the effect of exercising a right to limit processing.
When a statement clarifies that information will not be shared as part of a broader limitation request, it defines the scope and practical meaning of the right to restrict processing.
A sentence explaining an operational step taken to honor a data subject's restriction request directly describes the right to limit use of personal information.
A sentence indicating that a data record is designated as not shareable serves to explain the mechanism by which the right to restrict use of personal data is operationalized.

A sentence that enumerates distinct types of automated tracking tools and describes what each one captures or observes about a user's on-site behavior is specifying categories of user-related information.
If a passage describes information being tied to a user's session or profile and later usable to customize or target that user, it is identifying categories of personal information being assembled.
When a sentence explains that a technology records a user's movements, preferences, or interactions across pages or over time, it is describing a collection mechanism for personal data.

A sentence is labeled as describing categories of personal information collected when it explicitly names the types of data gathered (e.g., browsing history, device usage, network details) even if not directly identifying an individual.
A sentence that explains the procedural steps a data controller will follow when an individual exercises a stated privacy right is a description of that right.
Including a caveat about an exception (e.g., when data are deemed accurate) is characteristic of a fuller description of a correction right.
Such a sentence typically follows an initial declaration of the right and provides actionable detail about its implementation.
The language about requesting documentation and the conditional correction based on accuracy marks the sentence as elaborating the conditions under which the right is fulfilled.
A sentence that explicitly states a consumer's ability to prohibit the sale of their personal information directly expresses the right to opt out of such sale.
A sentence that presents the right as an instruction the consumer can give to the business ('direct us not to') matches the standard formulation of an opt-out mechanism.
The presence of the phrase 'You have the right to' signals that the sentence is formally articulating a legal entitlement, which is characteristic of a rights description.
When a heading or phrase is immediately followed by a clause that explains the right to opt out of the sale of personal information, the heading serves as a description of that same opt-out right.
When the sentence names the specific action being refused (sale of personal information) and the actor (third parties), it corresponds one-to-one with the scope of the opt-out right.

A sentence that introduces a privacy right by name and then clarifies its practical effect (what the data subject can ask the controller to do) is best categorized according to that described action, here limiting use of personal information.

The presence of a dedicated heading like 'Right of Restriction' followed by an explanatory statement indicates the text is intended to inform the reader of a specific data subject entitlement, supporting a label that names the corresponding right.

A sentence containing phrasing such as 'you have the right to request that we limit the use of' directly signals a restriction or limitation on how personal information is processed, which maps to a right-to-limit-use description.

A clause that specifies the scope of the limitation—here, 'sensitive personal information'—strengthens the match to a description of limiting use, since the sentence defines both the right and its target data category.
A statement that explicitly affirms that consumers will not face discriminatory treatment for exercising their privacy rights directly conveys the existence and scope of a non-discrimination right.

Connecting the non-discrimination promise to the exercise of privacy rights under both law and policy clarifies that the right attaches specifically to those actions, making the sentence a description of that right.

A prominent heading such as 'Non-Discrimination Notice' followed by a pledge of non-discrimination serves to inform consumers of the right to be free from adverse treatment for asserting privacy rights, which matches the definition of the label.

The use of negated discrimination language (such as 'will not discriminate') signals a guarantee of equal treatment, which is characteristic of a description of a right to non-discrimination rather than a mere policy practice.

A sentence that explains a consumer's privacy control or preference mechanism in the context of California law is categorized as describing a right to know what personal information is collected, because it informs users of their ability to exercise oversight over data collection.

Sentences framed as informational explanations of how to opt out of or signal restrictions on data collection belong to the right-to-know category, since they directly address the user's awareness of and control over the personal information gathered.

When a disclosure paragraph defines a technical privacy feature (such as a browser signal) and explicitly ties it to the tracking of user activity, it serves the function of educating the user about the scope of data that may be collected, which aligns with a right-to-know description.
A sentence that explicitly denies engaging in a particular data practice still falls under the category that names that practice, because it directly addresses the subject matter of that category.
A statement of non-disclosure or non-sale is a form of disclosure about the category, as it informs the reader about the organization's handling of that category.
The presence of the exact phrase 'personal information' and the verb 'sell' aligns the sentence with the label's semantic field, regardless of the negation.
When a label names a category of information or activity, any sentence that mentions the key terms of that category—even to state their absence—is classified under that category.

A concise action-oriented phrase describing an internal business operation indicates the processing of personal data in a business context, thereby contributing to the transparency required under data subject rights regarding collection and use.
A sentence that enumerates specific purposes for which data is used implicitly identifies the categories of personal information that must be collected to fulfill those purposes.

A label for a 'Description of Right to Know PI Collected' applies when the sentence explicitly grants an individual the ability to obtain an accounting of their collected personal information and its flow.

When a sentence appears as an item in a bulleted list following a preamble that explicitly states the organization's use of personal information for internal purposes, it functions as part of the disclosure of data handling practices, which is characteristic of a right-to-know notice.

A sentence that explicitly announces an arrangement where external entities are brought in to render services on behalf of the data collector describes a category of recipients for personal information.
A statement that makes recipients identifiable and notes the intended use of the data supports a consumer's understanding of their right to know about sale or sharing of personal information.
Explicitly naming contracted partners or third-party entities as recipients of personal information signals that the disclosure covers categories of data transferred to outside organizations.

Introductory phrasing that sets up a list of organizational purposes for which external parties receive data signals that the passage is part of a privacy notice's disclosure of information-sharing practices.

Language that frames the transfer as occurring for the collector's own operational benefit, rather than for the recipient's independent use, still constitutes a description of how personal information may be shared.

A sentence that discloses the specific business purposes or data-handling contexts in which personal information is involved falls under the category of describing the Right to Know PI sold or shared, because it informs the data subject about analytical uses of their information.

A sentence that enumerates categories of activities tied to processing personal information for operational or commercial reasons, without focusing on consumer rights or security measures, is properly labeled as a description of the Right to Know PI sold or shared.

Sentences that clarify the nature and scope of data use, including both marketing and non-marketing analytics, serve to satisfy transparency obligations about the transfer of personal information to other entities.

When a sentence lists functional activities such as analytics that are performed on personal information by or on behalf of the data controller, it constitutes a disclosure of how PI may be sold or shared with service providers or third parties.

A sentence that identifies which types of entities (e.g., service providers) receive personal information and specifies the exact subset of data transferred serves to describe the nature and scope of information sharing.

A statement that delineates boundaries on the data shared with service providers helps consumers understand which transfers are excluded from sale/sharing definitions and thereby defines the coverage of their opt-out rights.

A clause that conditions data provision on the necessity for performing a service clarifies whether the data transfer constitutes a business-purpose disclosure rather than an independent sale or sharing with third parties.

When a policy explains that only minimal information is given to operational vendors, it directly addresses consumers' right to know what personal information is disclosed and under what circumstances.

A sentence that restricts third parties from using personal information beyond a specified purpose indicates the entity retains control over how shared data is used, which relates to disclosures about data sharing practices.
Language clarifying the permissible scope of use by service providers addresses the conditions under which personal information is shared, a key element in fulfilling a right-to-know obligation.

A prohibition against unauthorized use by external parties signals that the sentence governs downstream handling of personal information, which is typically part of informing individuals about sale or sharing activities.

A provision stating that outside parties cannot use personal information except as authorized describes the limits placed on recipients of that data, which supports transparency about data flows subject to the right to know.
A sentence that explicitly states the entity may sell or disclose collected information directly addresses the consumer's right to know about the sale or sharing of personal information.

Distinguishing between service providers (who act on the company's behalf) and third parties (who do not provide services) is a hallmark of a disclosure about the right to know, as it clarifies the categories of recipients of personal information.

Using language that indicates the transfer of personal information for purposes beyond the company's own operations (such as marketing by others) signals that the sentence is informing consumers about data sharing or selling, a core component of the right to know.

A sentence that announces a policy is subject to change and explicitly signals that revisions are possible indicates that the policy has a forward-looking amendment provision, which is a hallmark of an updated policy notice.
A sentence that explicitly describes how users will be informed of revisions to a policy indicates the policy is subject to change, which supports the 'Updated Privacy Policy' label.
The presence of a heading or phrase such as 'CHANGES TO THE PRIVACY POLICY' directly indicates that the content addresses modifications, aligning with the label.

When a sentence contains both an explicit change-related heading and a declaration that the policy is subject to change, it clearly frames the content as a revision notice, which is a distinguishing feature of an updated privacy policy.
When a sentence explains the mechanism for identifying a revised policy and when the revision takes effect, it serves to inform users about updates to the document.
A sentence that explicitly states the policy may be revised in the future signals that the policy is subject to updates, warranting an 'Updated Privacy Policy' label.
A sentence that informs readers about the procedure for implementing changes to a policy is a strong indicator that the content is labeled as an updated policy statement.
Sentences that explicitly state the right to modify a policy or notice at any time indicate that the document's terms are subject to future change, which is characteristic of an updated policy.
When a policy document includes a section about how changes are posted and refers to a version date, a sentence providing that exact date functions as the formal notification of an update.
Sentences that specify that changes become effective immediately upon posting are characteristic of the updated policy label, as they define the implementation of revisions.
The inclusion of language about posting changes on the site and the immediate effectiveness of those changes indicates that the sentence serves to inform users of policy updates.
A sentence that establishes how and when users will be considered to have consented to modifications is characteristic of a policy-change notification section.
Provisions explaining how and when amended terms become binding on users are typical markers of policy-update content.
Language invoking constructive notice—where continued use implies consent to revisions—signals that the text belongs to an updated-policy section.
Language that ties acceptance of revisions to continued use of a service signals that the clause belongs to the declared 'changes' subsection rather than to informational or substantive policy terms.
Sentences that describe a mechanism by which users accept modifications through ongoing conduct are characteristic of policy-change notifications.
Statements that pair the effective timing of revisions with the resulting legal consequence for users are typical of update announcements in legal disclosure documents.
Text that frames acceptance as occurring automatically via future behavior reflects the notice language used when announcing policy revisions.
A sentence expressing automatic consent upon a specified user action (continued use) forms part of the standard mechanism for implementing policy amendments.

A sentence that explicitly names a data class, such as 'Personal Information,' and attaches operational conditions to it indicates that the text is delineating the categories of data an organization handles.

Detailing how long a named information type is retained implies that the organization actually collects and maintains that category, since only data that is gathered can be subject to a retention schedule.

Specifying retention windows and the circumstances under which they apply (such as after a relationship ends) clarifies the scope and lifecycle of a personal data category within the collection and handling framework.

When a policy sentence quantifies the persistence of a distinct data type, it helps readers identify which categories of personal information fall within the collector's practices, even when framed around storage rather than initial collection.
A sentence that explicitly promises not to discriminate against consumers for exercising their privacy rights directly states and thereby describes the right to non-discrimination.
In privacy policies, a dedicated notice that consumers will not be penalized for asserting their privacy choices typically fulfills legal obligations to describe the right to non-discrimination.

Statements disclaiming financial incentives, price differences, or service variations tied to personal data are integral to non-discrimination disclosures, since such differences could otherwise amount to discriminatory practices.

When a provision combines an anti-discrimination assurance with a financial-incentive disclaimer, both elements serve to inform consumers of protection from differential treatment and thus fall under the same non-discrimination right.
A sentence that explicitly names a consumer privacy right in its heading and then elaborates on what that right allows the consumer to do is classified as a description of that right.
Explaining the mechanism for exercising the right and the scope of data to which it applies marks the sentence as a functional description rather than a general notice.
Mentioning the governing privacy law or statute that grants the opt-out entitlement signals that the text is explaining the right itself.

When a sentence contains the phrase 'opt out' in connection with ceasing the 'sale' of personal information and explains the consequence (no longer selling and instead suppressing data), it directly characterizes the right to opt out of a sale.

A sentence referencing a data privacy law and specifying that it enables individuals to obtain information about how their personal details were given to outside entities for marketing aligns with the classification of a right to know about personal information sold or shared.

A sentence that cites a specific legal statute and explains that it grants certain individuals the right to request information about how their personal data is shared with third parties directly describes a consumer right to know about that sharing or sale.

Statements that outline a statutory mechanism for consumers to inquire about a company's disclosure of personal data to external companies for commercial or promotional reasons indicate the label for a right to know about personal information being sold or shared.

If a sentence frames the ability to ask about third-party marketing disclosures as a legal grant to certain residents, it is labeling that provision as a description of a right to know about the sale or sharing of personal information.

The label 'Description of Right to Know PI sold / shared' applies to sentences that articulate the circumstances under which personal information is collected and used, including the legal justifications that permit such sharing.

Legal or policy language that presents an opt-in or request mechanism regarding third-party marketing uses of personal data is characteristically a description of a data subject's right to be informed about such uses.

Text that specifies who is eligible (e.g., residents who provided personal information) and what they may inquire about (e.g., disclosures for marketing) functions as a description of a right to know rather than a mere summary of business practices.
A description of a right includes the scope of the right, such as what information it covers and from whom it can be requested.
Mentioning a specific legal framework and the timeframe for compliance shows the text is informing the consumer about the substance of their entitlement.
A passage that enumerates conditions under which the right does not apply is characteristic of a disclosure that describes the right, not a claim of action taken.
The presence of enumerated exceptions to the right indicates that the text is explaining the boundaries of the right rather than stating a policy or procedure.

A sentence that functions as a section heading and names a specific consumer right is best labeled as a description of that right, since it identifies the right rather than explaining its conditions or exceptions.

A sentence that articulates a statutory or regulatory right for individuals to obtain details about the disclosure of their personal information to third parties constitutes a description of a right to know about such sharing or selling.

Statements that break down the disclosure into distinct categories—such as sales versus business-purpose disclosures—indicate the sentence functions as a specification of what the right entails rather than a mere notice or policy statement.

The presence of a conditional trigger (e.g., 'If we sold...') followed by the procedural output of separate lists signals that the text explains the mechanism and content of a consumer's access right over commercial data transfers.

When a sentence details the substantive information a consumer would receive (which recipient obtained which categories), it is characterizing the scope of the right to know rather than the administrative steps to exercise it.

A sentence that enumerates the procedural steps the service will take upon receiving a verified deletion request, such as removing the data within a legally mandated timeframe, constitutes a description of the right to delete rather than merely a promise to honor it.
A sentence that explicitly states a user may request deletion of their personal data is classified as a description of the right to delete.

Descriptions of consumer privacy rights characteristically define the scope of the data covered, identify the categories of exceptions that permit retention, and state the obligations of the data controller—these structural elements together mark the text as a rendition of the right itself.

If a clause details both the affirmative right and the legally recognized carve-outs, it is not a mere notification of a policy but a substantive explanation of the right to deletion, thereby earning the label 'Description of Right to Delete'.

When the language frames the entitlement from the perspective of the consumer ('you have the right to request that we delete...') and then elaborates on what the business may or may not do, it is a canonical articulation of a rights description as seen in privacy policies.

A sentence that enumerates the concrete categories of information falling under the right (categories collected, sources, business purposes, and specific pieces) serves to spell out what the right covers, thereby describing the right's content and boundaries.

A sentence that opens by directly conferring an entitlement on the subject (e.g., 'You have the right to...') and then detailing what that entitlement lets the subject do is most naturally interpreted as a description of that right, not as a procedure, notice, or policy statement.

Referring to a defined lookback window (such as the preceding twelve months) and to activities performed on data (collection and use) indicates the sentence is delineating the temporal and substantive reach of a data-access right.

When a right is characterized as one to 'know and see' specific data items, the sentence functions to define the scope of an access-and-disclosure right, which is the hallmark of a Right-to-Know description rather than a deletion, correction, or opt-out right.

When a sentence itemizes the elements a data subject may request, it clarifies the subject matter that the disclosed right affords access to, making the sentence an expository description of that right rather than a limitation or exception to it.

A sentence that ties a user's ability to make changes to their account's personal data to a stated expectation or duty constitutes a description of the right to correct information, as it clearly communicates how the right is exercised.
A sentence that explicitly states that an individual may request correction of inaccurate data directly describes the right to correct information.
The use of action verbs such as 'correct' or 'update' in direct relation to personal data signals a focus on the user's correction rights.

Articulating the right to correct information typically involves naming both the data subject (as the actor) and the specific data object (personal data in an account), which together signal that the sentence is a statement of that right rather than a general policy note.

When a privacy policy assigns responsibility to the user for maintaining the accuracy of their personal data, it is functionally describing the right to correct information, because it acknowledges and enables the individual's control over data quality.
When a sentence ties the prohibition of discrimination to the act of exercising other specified rights, it constitutes a description of the non-discrimination right in that context.
A sentence that explicitly states a right to be free from discrimination when exercising other rights is classified as a description of that right.
Directive language like 'You have the right to not be discriminated against' indicates a formal statement of a legal or policy protection, which is characteristic of a rights description.
The presence of a phrase referencing previously stated rights, such as 'rights listed above,' signals that the sentence describes a protective condition attached to the exercise of those rights.

A sentence that explicitly enumerates specific communication channels or submission procedures for users to invoke their privacy rights is categorized as detailing the methods to exercise those rights.
Content that guides the user toward designated opt-out channels in order to realize an expressed choice belongs to the category of rights-exercise methods.
The presence of actionable directives such as 'please follow the instructions' or 'click here' signals that the sentence describes a concrete mechanism available to the user.
When a sentence indicates how a user can enforce a stated preference—such as ceasing receipt of marketing communications—it functions as a method for exercising that right.
A sentence that describes the transfer of collected information to external entities for operational or verification purposes is a disclosure of the categories of personal information sold or shared.

A sentence that enumerates the types of third-party recipients (e.g., marketing, advertising, payment providers) with whom information is shared, when appearing in a disclosure about sales, serves to specify the categories of personal information that may be sold.

The label 'Categories of Personal Information Sold' applies to sentences that enumerate distinct types of personal data a business may handle, regardless of whether the sentence explicitly mentions selling, because the label classifies the data type itself.

The inclusion of specific examples of service providers (e.g., phone number verification, email services) signals that the sentence is detailing the categories of personal information that may be sold or shared.

When a sentence enumerates the recipients of personal information and the conditions under which the transfer occurs, it falls under the label that categorizes the personal information involved in such transfers.

A disclosure that explicitly mentions transferring information during a merger, acquisition, or sale of assets indicates the data may be sold to another entity, warranting classification under sale categories.
Text that describes the disposition of data as an asset during corporate transactions signals that personal information may be exchanged as part of the deal, which falls under sale categories.

The presence of terms such as 'disclose,' 'transferred,' and 'asset transfer' in a statement is a hallmark of text that identifies the categories of personal information subject to sharing or disclosure.
A sentence mentioning bankruptcy or asset sale implies commercial transfer of data, making it relevant to categories of personal information sold even if no explicit monetary exchange is stated.
A sentence that cites a specific statutory provision and describes a legal entitlement granted to a defined class of individuals signals a description of a right to limit use of personal information.
Language framing the provision as something that 'permits' or 'allows' the data subject to take action indicates a facilitative privacy right rather than a mere policy statement.

Mentioning the ability to request information about or opt out of disclosures to third parties for marketing purposes is a hallmark of a privacy right that restricts secondary uses of personal information.
Specifying the eligible population (e.g., residents of a particular state) ties the described right to a particular legal jurisdiction and consumer-protection context.

A sentence that details the concrete steps taken to modify or deidentify personal information before sharing it with third parties functions to inform data subjects of their rights regarding the transfer or sale of their personal data.

Descriptions of steps that reduce the identifiability of data before external sharing, particularly when they specify the types of identifiers removed, are indicative of notices that explain the conditions under which personal information may be shared or sold.

Sentences that articulate the measures used to strip identifying details from information before it leaves the organization reflect a privacy disclosure obligation, making them classifiable as descriptions of the right to know about personal information that is shared or sold.

A passage that distinguishes between information that can be deidentified and information that can only be modified, while explaining the modification process, is characteristic of a statement outlining the data subject's right to be informed about what happens to their data prior to its disclosure to external parties.

When a statement lists specific data elements (such as name, account number, or address) that are removed prior to disclosure, it serves as a transparent explanation of how the data controller handles information that cannot be fully aggregated or deidentified, thereby describing the individual's right to know about such practices.
A sentence that explicitly states a last-modified date functions as metadata signaling the version and update status of a legal document.

The label 'Updated Privacy Policy' is appropriate for a sentence that serves as a temporal marker distinguishing the current version from prior ones; such markers are typically bare dates with no additional contextual prose.
The presence of a revision timestamp in the header of a policy document implies that the content has been modified or superseded, thereby marking it as an updated version.
In documents labeled as updated privacy policies, dated revision markers serve to certify that the current version supersedes earlier ones and is the one in effect.
The inclusion of a 'Last updated' date at the top of a privacy policy signals that the document has a version history and reflects its most recent revision.
Privacy policies commonly feature a prominent date stamp to inform readers when the most recent revision occurred, distinguishing it from the policy's substantive terms.
The presence of a specific date combined with the phrase 'Last Modified' is a strong indicator that the document has been updated, making it appropriate for a label denoting an updated policy.
A sentence that states an explicit effective or revision date using a phrase like 'Last updated' serves as the official marker of a policy's most recent modification.
When the sentence links the non-discrimination guarantee to the exercise of other specified rights, it signals a right-to-non-discrimination statement.

A sentence that enumerates specific prohibited actions (such as refusal of service, price variation, or quality differences) in relation to consumer rights is functioning as a description of a non-discrimination safeguard.
The explicit listing of dimensions where discrimination is barred (denial, pricing, quality) signals that the sentence characterizes the breadth of a non-discrimination right.
A sentence phrased as a direct assurance of equal treatment, conditional on consumer action, is substantively a description of a right to non-discrimination.
A sentence that prescribes the specific format, required content, or procedural steps for submitting a privacy-related request is classified as describing a method to exercise rights.
A sentence that instructs a data subject on what identifying details to include when submitting a formal privacy request is describing a method for exercising their rights.

Content that explains what information will be requested from the user to verify identity during a consumer rights request belongs to the methods to exercise rights label, as it instructs on how to proceed with exercising those rights.

When a sentence details the post-request verification requirements, it forms part of the method for exercising rights, distinguishing the logistics of the request from the substantive rights themselves.

A sentence that addresses consumer preferences regarding data deletion versus sale suppression, and explains why a business clarifies the type of request, is describing the right to opt out of the sale of personal information.

A sentence that clarifies the distinction between a request to delete data and a request to opt out of data sales, and explains the operational purpose of opt-out (e.g., suppression), is characteristic of a description of the right to opt out of sale of personal information.
A sentence that explicitly affirms the user's ability to make a choice regarding the sale of their personal information is a description of the right to opt out.

Content that explains the practical effect of an opt-out—maintaining data to block future sales—rather than guaranteeing its deletion, is a hallmark of a clause detailing the right to opt out of sale.

A sentence that explicitly announces a taxonomy or grouping of data types acts as a structural heading for the subsequent enumeration of those types, which is characteristic of passages that disclose categories of personal information.

Even if a sentence contains no concrete data points itself, its role as a prologue to a set of items that are characterized as collected makes it an integral element of the section that categorizes personal information.

A lead-in sentence that precedes a bulleted or sequential list of data subcategories contributes to the label of 'categories' because it establishes the scope and subdivisions of the personal information handling discussion.

The use of phrasing that signals a classification, such as mentioning 'types' of a data artifact, frames the following details as belonging to a known category of collected information even before specific examples are given.

When a sentence introduces a set of distinct items that are described as being collected or processed, it semantically organizes the disclosure into named classes, thereby functioning as part of the 'categories of personal information collected' discourse.

A sentence that serves as a section heading and begins with the phrase 'Right to ...' followed by a specific legal entitlement is conventionally used to state or name that right, making it a description of the right itself rather than an implementation detail.

Informing users that they are subject to another party's privacy policy is a way of describing the circumstances under which personal information may be collected, which is part of a right-to-know disclosure.

When a document lists rights and then provides explanatory paragraphs, each listed entry that serves as a title for subsequent details is considered part of the description of the corresponding right, regardless of whether the entry itself contains explanatory content.

A sentence that serves as a section heading and begins with the phrase 'Right to ...' followed by a specific legal entitlement is conventionally used to state or name that right, making it a description of the right itself rather than an implementation detail.
A short enumerative item gains its classification from the substantive content of the right it references, not from the length or grammatical completeness of the sentence itself.
Even a terse or fragmentary phrase can receive this label if its referent right, as elaborated elsewhere in the document, is centrally about transparency of collected personal information.

A label for a 'Description of Right to Know PI Collected' applies when the sentence explicitly grants an individual the ability to obtain an accounting of their collected personal information and its flow.

When a right's legal or policy definition involves the ability to request disclosure of categories or sources of personal data, the sentence naming that right is mapped to the 'right to know PI collected' category.

A sentence that stands alone as a list item naming a specific consumer right over personal data is categorized by the purpose that the surrounding document assigns to the list as a whole, since the label reflects the functional role of the item within that context.

If a document groups several rights under an introduction that frames them as rights related to a consumer's control over or knowledge of collected personal information, then each item in that grouping inherits that framing for annotation purposes regardless of the item's own verbosity.

The presence of a noun-phrase structure such as 'The right of X' signals a distinct legal entitlement; in a data-protection policy, such entitlements are annotated according to the type of personal-information relationship they govern, even if the phrase itself lacks explanatory detail.

When a policy enumerates multiple rights and then explicitly states they are covered by the same policy, each listed right is treated as belonging to the same overarching category as the rights that receive explicit descriptive elaboration.

A sentence that explicitly references the privacy policy and appears within a group of statements enumerating the purposes of collection, categories of third parties, and specific pieces of personal information is classified as describing the consumer's right to know about the sale or sharing of that information.
Sentences structured as a list of user entitlements, introduced by a phrase like 'The right to...', signal a description of a specific privacy right rather than a policy obligation or data practice.

When a sentence appears as a concise bullet point within a document that introduces a series of data protection rights, it is interpreted under the umbrella of the right to know about personal information processing, even if the sentence itself names no specific data categories.

A sentence that articulates a specific data subject right using a noun phrase beginning with 'The right to' and that is listed among other data privacy rights is typically categorized as a description of a consumer right related to personal information, especially when the right concerns a processing activity that relies on collected data.

In a privacy policy where rights are enumerated as discrete statements, each statement that guarantees protection against a type of data processing serves as a detailed explanation of the general transparency rights a consumer holds over their personal information.

A right concerning automated decision-making is logically grouped with the right to know about collected personal information because automated decisions are made using that information, and an individual must be informed of such processing to assert this right.

When a list of rights includes items that all pertain to how personal data is handled, those items collectively flesh out the scope of the right to know, so a sentence about automated decision-making is a natural specification of that broader right.

A sentence that names a user-initiated action to stop a specific form of data processing (such as targeted advertising) describes a right to limit the use of personal information.

When a sentence references a recognized self-regulatory program for advertising opt-outs, it informs the user of a specific channel to restrict use of their personal data, consistent with a right-to-limit description.
A sentence that directs users to a platform where they can manage their advertising preferences constitutes a description of the right to limit use of personal information.

A sentence whose purpose is to direct readers to an external application or webpage for controlling targeted advertising functions as a description of the right to restrict data processing.
A sentence that serves as a heading or lead-in to further details about opt-out or limitation mechanisms is part of the description of the right to limit use of personal information.
A sentence that explicitly names a consumer control over sensitive personal information, such as limiting its processing, is classified as describing the right to limit use of personal information.

When a sentence describes segmenting individuals based on shared traits or behavior, it signals that the collector obtains data about those traits or behaviors, making the statement relevant to describing the categories of personal data handled.
A sentence that lists a discrete type of information as an item within an enumeration is best classified under the same category label that governs the entire enumeration.

A sentence that enumerates specific circumstances or purposes under which personal data is shared with third parties directly supports labeling it as a category of information shared or disclosed.

When a sentence provides actionable guidance, such as directing the reader to complete a specific form or use a concrete channel, it is classified as a method rather than a mere statement of rights.

Descriptions of requirements that must be satisfied to validate a request belong to the explanation of how to exercise the applicable rights.

When a sentence references earlier text for details, it links to the comprehensive instructions that constitute the methods for submitting rights requests.

A sentence that prescribes a specific procedure or channel (e.g., a form, email, or portal) for taking an action classified as a privacy right falls under the label for methods of exercising that right.
If a sentence provides the concrete means (channel, address, format) by which a data subject can take action on their privacy choice, it serves the function of explaining how to exercise that right.
Instructions that mandate the use of a particular email address and subject line to submit an appeal are characteristic of content describing the exercise of privacy rights.
When a sentence tells the reader what they must do (e.g., submit a request using an exact subject line or email address) to act on a right, it belongs to a section explaining how to exercise rights.

A sentence is labeled as a method for exercising rights when it specifies concrete procedural actions, such as submitting a form or contacting a designated address, that a user must take to invoke a privacy right.

Text that ties a stated limitation right to state-specific definitions of sensitive information indicates the disclosure is explaining a particular consumer privacy right rather than making a general policy statement.

When a heading or lead-in names a specific consumer control, such as limiting processing of sensitive data, the accompanying text that explains the organization's handling of that data serves the same descriptive purpose.

Verbs granting permission or agency, such as 'may' or 'can,' signal the availability of a user-initiated procedure and therefore indicate a description of an opt-out right.

A sentence specifying a business operational purpose, such as product debugging to restore intended functionality, functions as an exemption statement that is grammatically and thematically part of the right-to-delete explanation.

A sentence that specifies exceptions or conditions under which an entity may decline to fully act on a consumer request serves to define the scope of that right, and is therefore part of its description.

Sentences enumerating permissible grounds for retaining personal data are typical components of a data-deletion disclosure, because such disclosures are structured as a list of exceptions to the deletion obligation.

A sentence appearing within a sequence of items that follow an introduction of a consumer right and its verification procedure is categorized under that same right, as it continues the same enumerated structure.

A sentence describing a condition under which a service provider may deny a requested action is a defining component of the right being described, because it delineates the limits of that entitlement.

A sentence that explicitly names a specific right using the phrase 'Right to ...' directly identifies that right, making it a description of that right.
When a sentence functions as a section heading and is immediately followed by content elaborating the mechanics of that right, it is typically labeled as the description of that right.
If the sentence uses the exact terminology expected for the right (e.g., 'Correct Your Inaccurate Personal Information'), it unambiguously indicates that the labeled right is the subject matter.

When a sentence closely paraphrases and expands upon a section heading from the same document, it is usually serving as the explanatory content for that heading, warranting a label matching the heading's topic.
A sentence that conditions the corrective action on verification of the request and then explains the ensuing remedy is characterizing the operational details of the asserted correction right.
A sentence that outlines the concrete actions an organization will take when a user invokes a privacy right can be categorized as a description of that right.

The presence of an explicit commitment to act (e.g., using 'commercially reasonable efforts') signals that the sentence is describing how the right will be honored, not merely restating the right itself.
When a sentence tailors a general right by including conditions or exceptions (such as impossibility or excessive effort), it further specifies the right's scope and boundaries.
A sentence that explicitly states the absence of negative treatment for lawful actions is typically categorized as a description of a non-discrimination right.
When a sentence links a protected activity (exercising privacy rights) to a safeguard against adverse or unequal treatment, it serves to characterize the corresponding non-discrimination protection.
The inclusion of the rights holder's perspective ('you') and the protected action makes the sentence an explanatory description of the right itself.
Using prohibitive language such as 'will not discriminate' indicates the sentence is articulating a right rather than stating a policy condition or exception.
A sentence that explicitly names a consumer privacy right in its heading and then elaborates on what that right allows the consumer to do is classified as a description of that right.

A sentence that states a consumer's entitlement to instruct a business to restrict processing of a specific data category directly constitutes a description of the right to limit the use of that personal information.
Describing both 'use' and 'disclosure' of information aligns with the scope of a limit-use right, as it covers internal processing and external sharing.

When a sentence narrows the described right to a specific data category, such as sensitive personal information, it serves to define the scope of the right and thus functions as a description of that right.
The phrasing 'You may have the right to request' signals that the statement is articulating a user-facing right rather than a business obligation or procedural detail.

A sentence that describes procedural requirements or exemptions for submitting a data-related consumer request is classified under methods for exercising rights.
Clarifying the absence of an administrative precondition (such as account creation) for acting on privacy rights constitutes part of the stated methodology.
Guidance that informs individuals how they can initiate or complete an action regarding their personal data falls within the category of methods to exercise rights.

Statements that justify data retention by referencing the need to provide ongoing services serve to identify exceptions to a deletion request, and thus are considered descriptive of the deletion right.

When a passage about the right to delete lists permissible retention purposes, any sentence that adds another such purpose belongs to the same category, as it further defines when deletion is not required.

A sentence that explains the practical consequences or limitations that follow from exercising a stated privacy right is considered part of the description of that right, because the description is incomplete without noting downstream effects.

If a sentence is placed within a section detailing the right to delete and it elaborates on what happens after deletion is performed, it extends that description rather than introducing a separate topic.

In a privacy notice, any statement that specifies a condition under which a deletion request can be denied serves to clarify the boundaries of the offered deletion right, making it an inherent component of that right's description.

When a sentence directly addresses the user's request to take an action (such as deleting personal information) and then specifies how that action impacts their ability to use a service, it clarifies the scope of the right and thus falls under the label for that right.

When a sentence provides enumerated or alternative procedural options (such as submitting a request online or calling a number) for enforcing a right, it conveys the available methods for that right.

When a sentence identifies the right holder (the individual or their authorized agent) and the action they may take (request correction), it serves to communicate the existence and scope of the corrective right.

Sentences that detail proactive measures for data accuracy complement the procedural steps for correction requests, making them classifiable under the same right.

A statement that commits the data holder to maintaining accurate records directly supports the data subject's right to request corrections, since a correction right is meaningless without an ongoing duty of data accuracy.

A statement that identifies the legal basis (such as state law) for processing certain data and then clarifies the non-availability of a corresponding opt-out mechanism still communicates the scope and existence of the right.

When a statement frames an action as a right the individual 'has the right to request,' it signals a formal description of a data protection entitlement.
Including qualifiers about the nature of the data and processing purposes indicates the scope and conditions attached to the correction right.
