A sentence that explicitly states an individual's entitlement to have inaccurate personal data amended or rectified is categorized as a description of the right to correct information.
A sentence that uses the explicit construction 'You have the right to...' followed by an action directly articulates a consumer entitlement, making it a description of that right.

Sentences that name the specific data subject ('personal information collected and maintained about you') while tying it to a removal request are characteristic of documents enumerating data subject rights.
The presence of scope qualifiers such as 'on a device-by-device basis' or similar limitations modifies the extent of the right without altering its fundamental nature as a deletion right.
When a sentence specifies the action of removing personal data and identifies that data as belonging to the user, it expresses the core content of the right to delete, justifying the label.
A sentence that identifies the category of personal information governed by a stated right serves to describe the scope of that right.
In a privacy disclosure, language defining which data triggers a consumer control is treated as part of the description of that control's right to limit use.
When a document presents consecutive statements about a right, earlier sentences framing the subject matter are understood to describe that right's applicability.
A sentence located within a dedicated section of a privacy notice is read as elaborating the right announced by that section's heading.
A sentence that defines the boundaries of a company's consent obligations for processing sensitive data directly describes the scope of a consumer's right to limit that processing.
Addressing consent for 'sensitive personal information' maps directly onto the consumer-facing right to limit use and disclosure of that same category of data.
Explaining that an obligation is contingent on the effectiveness of specific laws clarifies the conditions and extent of the right being described.
Language that curtails a company's processing duties functions as an explanation of the parameters of the right to restrict data use, not as a grant of a separate right.
Tying an obligation to what is required under corresponding state privacy laws specifies the precise limits of how a stated privacy right will apply.
A sentence that prescribes a specific contact channel for submitting a request constitutes a concrete directive for exercising the rights described in the surrounding text.
Sentences specifying a destination address or medium for a user-initiated action are classified as methods for carrying out the legal or policy-based entitlements.
When a document enumerates multiple avenues for action, each sentence that names an actionable step qualifies as a method to exercise the referenced rights.

A sentence that defines or analogizes a data-collection technology, such as by comparing it to another known tracking mechanism, is describing the methods through which personal information is gathered, thereby categorizing it as personal information collected.

A statement that identifies a technology as the mobile equivalent of a web-based tracker indicates that user data is being captured on devices, which falls under the classification of collected personal information.

If the surrounding text enumerates data-gathering tools (like cookies or pixels) and a sentence extends that enumeration to a related form, the sentence is part of a taxonomy of personal information collection methods.

When a sentence clarifies how a tracking technology operates (e.g., its scope or platform variant), it contributes to enumerating the categories of personal information that a system may collect from users.

A sentence that explicitly references a specific consumer privacy statute and delineates a temporal window for the personal information collected is characteristic of a disclosure addressing the right to know what data is gathered.

A sentence that points users to other sections for the detailed disclosures of collected information and purposes serves as a description of the right to know, as it directs them to the operative content for that right.

The inclusion of statutory triggers (e.g., a privacy law acronym) alongside categories of data and purposes signals that the sentence is fulfilling an obligation to describe the right to know personal information collected.

When a sentence enumerates both the personal information collected and the business or commercial purposes for its use, it directly mirrors the core elements of the right-to-know requirement under privacy regulations.

A sentence that explicitly states the user holds a right to take a specific action—such as opting out of a data practice—functions as a direct description of that right, regardless of surrounding clauses.

If a sentence references limiting the processing or use of a specific category of personal data (here, Sensitive PI) and explains how a user can invoke that limitation, it is naturally classified as a description of the right to limit use.
Phrasing that ties the described action to an external rights procedure indicates the sentence functions as an explanation of a particular consumer entitlement.
A sentence framed around what the data subject 'has the right to' do, rather than what the company will do, belongs to a taxonomy of user-right descriptions.

A statement describing recognition of a user across separate visits indicates that the site collects stored attributes of that user, which falls under the category of personal information maintained about the individual.

In a list of purposes for automatically gathered data, a purpose that depends on linking the current session to a prior visit reveals that the data collected is tied to an identifiable individual rather than being purely anonymous.
Privacy-policy language explaining that personal data is available to other users or customers serves to notify about disclosed categories of personal information.

The capability to recognize a returning user entails the use of persistent identifiers such as cookies or device fingerprints, and these identifiers are a category of personal information collected from that user.
A sentence that explains the legal grounds for processing personal data serves to inform individuals about why their information may be used, which is a core component of transparency rights.
A statement that references the lawful bases for processing directly addresses the disclosure obligations that enable individuals to know what justifies the collection and use of their personal data.

Explaining that processing depends on the type of information and specific circumstances delineates the scope of an organization's data practices, which is essential for a meaningful description of an individual's right to be informed.

Identifying that the applicable legal basis depends on context and data type describes the conditions under which collection occurs, supporting a data subject's right to understand how their personal information is handled.

Sentences that specify factors determining when processing is permitted provide the contextual detail needed to satisfy requirements for describing the right to know what personal information is collected and why.
A sentence that directs users to an external resource for instructions on deleting or controlling cookies typically offers a practical method for users to enforce their privacy preferences.
Indicating where users can find steps to remove or manage cookies constitutes a procedural avenue for them to act on their stated rights, fitting the category of methods to exercise rights.
When a document addresses user rights regarding data and tracking, a statement that points to guidance on managing those technologies is classified as a method for exercising those rights.

A sentence that introduces additional or secondary uses of personal information not originally specified helps fulfill the obligation to inform data subjects of the full scope of processing activities.
Concise headings or phrases that signal constraints on future data usage directly relate to the transparency required for individuals to exercise their right to know about collected data.

Language indicating that stored personal data may be applied to compatible new purposes addresses the individual's entitlement to understand how their collected information may subsequently be employed.
Statements that qualify the boundaries of permissible data processing contribute to the description of the data subject's right to be informed about collection and usage.
A sentence states a legal limitation on a user's data request, which explains the scope of the user's right to know their collected personal data.
Language describing when a request may be denied directly addresses the conditions and exceptions governing the disclosed right.
Phrasing that frames a potential refusal as permitted or required by law clarifies the boundaries of the user's entitlement to the requested information.
A label describing a data-subject right applies when the sentence states an actionable option available to the individual concerning their own data.
A sentence that explicitly states that an individual may request correction of inaccurate data directly describes the right to correct information.
Statements that define what a person can ask the data controller to do regarding data accuracy are classified as descriptions of rights rather than obligations or policy notices.
The presence of the verb 'request' coupled with the object 'inaccurate personal information' signals a remedial action the organization permits the user to initiate.
Sentences that frame the right in terms of user-initiated requests, rather than company obligations or exceptions, are classified as descriptions of the right itself.
A sentence that explicitly states a user may request deletion of their personal data is classified as a description of the right to delete.

In privacy policy contexts, any sentence that names both the user's power to initiate removal of personal information and the subject of that action (personal information) is typically categorized as a description of the right to delete.

The presence of the phrase 'personal information' paired with an explicit request action (e.g., 'delete') in a user-facing statement signals that the sentence is informing the user of a legally recognized deletion right.

When a statement uses direct, actionable language (e.g., 'you can request') to describe an action a user may take regarding their own data, it functions as a description of a user right rather than a procedural or consequential note.

A sentence that explains the practical consequences or limitations that follow from exercising a stated privacy right is considered part of the description of that right, because the description is incomplete without noting downstream effects.
Descriptions of a right often include caveats or post-processing conditions to set expectations, thus belonging to the same category as the core right.
Statements that clarify what happens after a request is fulfilled, such as loss of access to prior services, elaborate on the scope of the right being discussed.
When a sentence directly addresses the effects of a deletion request, it serves to inform the user of the practical implications of the deletion right.
A sentence that mentions a protected action (like exercising privacy rights) in connection with a promise of equal treatment is recognized as a description of the right to non-discrimination.
A sentence that explicitly states a right to be free from discrimination when exercising other rights is classified as a description of that right.
The inclusion of a clause that ties the non-discrimination guarantee to applicable laws indicates that the sentence is establishing a legal right rather than merely expressing a policy aspiration.
A sentence that explicitly states that the exercise of other enumerated rights is protected from discriminatory treatment is directly describing a right to non-discrimination.
A sentence that instructs users on specific actions to take to exercise their privacy rights is classified as describing methods to exercise rights.
Sentences that explicitly reference procedural resources or steps for submitting a rights request are categorized as providing methods to exercise rights.
When a document first announces procedures for exercising rights, listing the categories of rights establishes the subject matter that those procedures address.
A sentence naming distinct user entitlements such as access, correction, deletion, or opt-out contributes to explaining how rights are exercised by clarifying what can be requested.
A statement that details the specific types of user activity monitored (like page popularity and navigation) indicates that the organization is collecting personal information through those cookies.

Language detailing the purpose of tracking tools, such as counting visits to improve performance, surfaces the type of information collected—namely internet or network activity—relevant to a categories-of-information label.

Sentences that describe mechanisms for counting user visits and tracking traffic sources indicate the collection of online activity or behavioral data, which falls within a category of personal information.

Statements explaining how site performance is measured through user interaction data signal the disclosure of the categories of personal information being gathered, rather than individual data points.
A classification of shared or disclosed categories applies when the text frames data flow in terms of who receives it and under what conditions, rather than how the data is processed internally.

The presence of scenario-based clauses covering legal compulsion, business transactions, and commercial partnerships indicates the text is mapping the full scope of entities that may receive personal information.

When a passage itemizes separate recipient groups — such as commercial partners, authorities, and transactional successors — it signals a categorical breakdown of disclosures rather than a single sharing event.
A sentence that enumerates distinct types of external parties or circumstances under which personal data is transferred is classified as describing categories of sharing or disclosure.

A sentence that frames the collection as happening 'over time' and 'across other sites' points to cross-context behavioral tracking, which data privacy frameworks treat as a form of selling or sharing because the information is made available to third parties for targeted advertising.

If the sentence indicates that information about the user's browsing is gathered across other sites and services, not just the current site, the label used for such a disclosure tends to be one that signals data monetization or a trade-like exchange, rather than a purely internal processing activity.

When a sentence explains that data is collected via third-party advertising networks or social media platforms specifically to tailor ads based on observed behavior, the disclosed practice is classified under a category that reflects the transfer or disclosure of personal information to third parties for commercial purposes.

A sentence describing the use of cookies or similar technologies to collect information about a user's activity across multiple sites and over time for interest-based advertising is typically categorized as 'sale' or 'sharing' of personal information under laws like the CCPA/CPRA.

A sentence that specifies a method or format by which an individual can obtain a copy of their personal data is a concrete elaboration of the broader right to know what information has been collected about them.

A statement granting a user the ability to request their information in a portable and usable way serves to fulfill the disclosure obligation, thereby constituting a description of the right to know the personal information collected.

The inclusion of a named statutory mechanism, such as 'data portability', signals that the sentence is describing a sub‑feature of the overarching transparency right to access one's collected personal information.

When a privacy notice first establishes a general entitlement to disclosure about collection and use, any later sentence that details how that entitlement can be exercised (such as through a specific delivery format) remains part of the same described right.
A sentence that explicitly states a user's ability to terminate participation or data collection at any time is classified as describing an opt-out right.
A statement that assures the user their choice is honored without delay falls under the description of the opt-out right.

The presence of conditional language such as 'under certain circumstances' signals a qualified right, which is characteristic of consumer privacy rights descriptions rather than absolute or operational statements.

When a sentence contains the phrase 'opt out' in connection with ceasing the 'sale' of personal information and explains the consequence (no longer selling and instead suppressing data), it directly characterizes the right to opt out of a sale.
A sentence that enumerates specific contact channels (such as postal address, web form, or phone number) for users to pursue data-related requests is classified under methods to exercise rights.

When a sentence directly follows an instruction describing how to exercise access, deletion, or portability rights and offers a practical avenue to do so, it is functioning as a procedural mechanism rather than a mere description of policy.

A sentence framed as an option within a set of alternatives (e.g., 'by either' followed by contact methods) indicates it belongs to a group of permissible ways to exercise those rights, not to a separate topic.

A sentence that establishes the legal or regulatory definition of the key term 'personal information' is a common preamble for disclosing the specific categories of such information that an organization collects.

A statement that acknowledges definitional variation across jurisdictions primes the reader for a subsequent breakdown of specific data traits, which aligns with the purpose of a 'categories collected' section.

Explicitly referencing multiple data-protection frameworks (like U.S. and EU laws) signals to readers that the following text will enumerate which data types fall under those distinct regulatory definitions, which is a core function of a categories-of-collected-data disclosure.

Introducing and defining an acronym (e.g., 'PI') in a policy typically precedes the structured categorization of what the acronym encompasses, making the sentence a natural fit for the heading under which it appears.

A clause that ties the sharing of non-identifying data to business or operational benefits demonstrates that the text is addressing the disclosure of information categories, which aligns with a disclosure-oriented label.

The presence of language indicating the data is given to others for purposes like product improvement or customer service signals that the sentence is specifying how information is shared or disclosed rather than merely collected.

A sentence that explicitly states the organization discloses or shares information to external parties, even when the data is anonymous or aggregated, directly describes a category of information sharing or disclosure.

When a statement frames information handling in terms of recipients and downstream uses, it functions to enumerate what types of data are shared or disclosed, even if the data itself is de-identified.
Wording that directly references the sharing or disclosure of personal information aligns with categories that describe the sale or transfer of such data.
A sentence that specifies an event (e.g., purchase or merger) triggering the transfer of personal data to another entity indicates that such data is being shared or disclosed to a third party.

A statement that situates data transfer within a corporate transaction context (like asset purchase) is categorized under disclosure, because it identifies a scenario in which personal information leaves the original controller's control.

In a privacy disclosure, a sentence that delineates a subcategory of collected data—such as a physiological or behavioral attribute—serves to enumerate the scope of information covered, thereby fitting the 'categories of personal information' label.
A sentence that pairs a named data-category term with concrete example fields acts as a definition of that category's scope.
A taxonomy-like heading followed by a colon and a list of data types signals that the sentence is categorizing personal information rather than describing collection methods or purposes.
When a sentence enumerates specific data elements without stating a policy or action, it functions purely as a classification of information types.
